newsitem.title: USA: CFTC chair sees improved audit trails at exchanges.
newsitem.headline: CFTC chair sees improved audit trails at exchanges.

text.p: The two largest U.S. futures exchanges still need to improve their record keeping procedures to provide audit trails of trading, the new chairwoman of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission said.
Chicago Board of Trade and the Chicago Mercantile Exchange are not meeting federally mandated standards for audit trails, chairwoman Brooksley Born said in an interview with Reuters.

"We certainly hope more progress can be made," Born said. "The Chicago exchanges are not yet in compliance and we've extended the period in which they should and are working closely with them to assist them in any way we can."
Born's comments echoed the conclusions of a report released this week by General Accounting Office on audit trails at the futures exchanges.
The GAO report found that while some exchanges are meeting the standards for audits trails, the CBOT and the CME are not.

A spokeswoman for the CME said the exchange's position has not changed since the CFTC issued a study on audit trails in August. At that time, CME president Bill Brodsky said the exchange could satisfy "any remaining concerns" about audit trails by January 1, 1997.
The CFTC is conducting a number of investigations and studies of matters at the exchanges and in U.S. commodity markets, Born said in the interview.
Ongoing probes include a look at the use of agricultural hedge-to-arrive contracts, the actions of for-profit broker groups and a probe of the copper market begun in late 1995, Born said.

The coper probe heated up after Sumitomo Corp announced in June that it had fired its top copper trader, Yasuo Hamanaka, after suffering losses of $1.8 billion. The firm revised its loss estimate to $2.6 billion last week.
"It is ongoing and it's proceeding as one would expect," Born said. "I think it is a complex area and it takes some time to complete this kind of investigation."

Born declined to discuss details of the probe. "I can't comment on who we are looking at," she said. "Obviously we are looking at any potential violations of the Commodity Exchange Act that we come across in the course of the investigation."
